essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to receive and check a delivery of products at a salon or spa.
essays.modelAnswer: When the driver arrives, I check that the delivery is for our salon and find our copy of the purchase order. Before I sign, I count the boxes and look for crushed, wet or leaking packages. Then I open the boxes and check each item against the delivery note and the purchase order: the right product, size, colour and number. I check the expiry dates and that the seals are not broken. If anything is short, wrong, damaged or out of date, I write it on the delivery note before I sign, keep the damaged items apart, and tell the supervisor so the supplier can be contacted. Then I enter the goods received on the stock cards or the computer system. Finally I put the stock away safely, with new stock behind the old, and chemicals in their proper store.
markingPoints: Checks the delivery is for the salon and finds the purchase order
Checks the packages for damage before signing
Checks each item, the quantity and the expiry dates against the delivery note and order
Records any shortage or damage on the note and reports it to the supervisor
Updates the stock records and puts stock away safely, using FIFO

essays.stem: Explain how a salon should store its products safely, including chemicals and products that can catch fire.
essays.modelAnswer: All products should be kept in a clean, cool, dry place out of direct sunlight, because heat and sun can spoil them, which matters in Jamaica's hot weather. Heavy items and large bottles go on the lower shelves so they are safe to lift and cannot fall. Products stay in their original containers with the labels showing, and lids are closed tightly. Chemicals such as relaxers, perm lotion, hair colour and peroxide are stored as their safety data sheets say, often in a locked cupboard away from clients and children, and kept below eye level. Flammable products such as acetone, nail polish, hairspray and some alcohol-based products are kept in a cool, ventilated place, away from heaters, dryers, flames and sparks, with no smoking nearby. The stock room is kept tidy, with clear walkways and a fire extinguisher close by.
markingPoints: Cool, dry, clean place out of direct sunlight and heat
Heavy and large items on the lower shelves
Original, labelled containers with lids closed
Chemicals stored as the SDS says, often locked and below eye level
Flammables away from heat and sparks, ventilated, with an extinguisher nearby

essays.stem: Explain what stock rotation (FIFO) means, how you would do it when putting away new stock, and why it is important.
essays.modelAnswer: Stock rotation means using or selling the older stock before the newer stock. It is often called FIFO, which stands for "first in, first out". When a new delivery arrives, I first check the dates on the stock already on the shelf. I move the older items to the front and put the new items behind them, or underneath them in the stock room. If a new item has an earlier expiry date than the old stock, the item with the earliest date goes to the front. I also check for any items that are already out of date or damaged, and take them off the shelf and record them. Rotation is important because beauty products can lose their quality over time. It stops products going out of date on the shelf, saves money, and means clients always receive products that are fresh and safe to use.
markingPoints: Explains FIFO: older stock is used or sold first
New stock goes behind or under the older stock
Checks dates, and the earliest expiry goes to the front
Removes and records out-of-date or damaged stock
Explains it reduces waste and keeps products fresh and safe

essays.stem: Describe how to carry out a stock take in a salon or spa.
essays.modelAnswer: A stock take is planned for a time when the salon is closed or quiet, so that no sales or deliveries happen during the count. Staff are given a stock sheet or list for their area, such as the retail shelves, the dispensary or the stock room. Each person counts shelf by shelf, in order, and writes each number down at once. Open items used at the basin may be counted as part bottles, as the salon's method says. A second person checks some of the counts. Then the counts are compared with the stock cards or the computer system. Any difference, called a variance, is checked again. Damaged and out-of-date items are counted separately and recorded. The value of the stock is worked out by multiplying the number of each item by its cost price. Finally the records are corrected, and the results and any losses are reported to the manager.
markingPoints: Done when closed or quiet, with stock sheets for each area
Counts shelf by shelf and records at once, with checks by a second person
Compares the counts with the stock records and rechecks differences
Records damaged or expired items separately and works out the stock value
Corrects the records and reports the results to the manager

essays.stem: Explain what minimum stock, maximum stock and the reorder level are, and how they help a salon decide when and how much to order. Use an example.
essays.modelAnswer: Minimum stock, or safety stock, is the smallest amount the salon should hold so it does not run out if a delivery is late or sales go up. Maximum stock is the most it wants to hold, so that money is not tied up and products do not expire. The reorder level is the stock level at which a new order is placed. It is the amount used during the delivery time plus the safety stock. For example, a salon uses 5 tubs of hair food a week, delivery takes 2 weeks and the safety stock is 4 tubs. The reorder level is 5 times 2, plus 4, which is 14 tubs. If the maximum is 30 tubs and there are 14 when the order is placed, the salon orders 16. Using these levels means the salon orders at the right time and in the right amount.
markingPoints: Explains minimum (safety) stock correctly
Explains maximum stock and why it limits the order
Explains the reorder level: usage during delivery time plus safety stock
Gives a correct worked example
Explains that this avoids running out and overstocking

essays.stem: Describe what you should do when you find stock that is damaged, faulty or out of date.
essays.modelAnswer: First I take the item off the shelf or out of use straight away, so that it is not sold or used on a client. If it is leaking or broken, I put on gloves, wipe up any spill safely as the safety data sheet says, and put out a wet floor sign. I keep the item in a marked area or box for damaged stock. I record it on the stock card or the damaged stock sheet, with the date, the product, the number and the reason. I report it to the supervisor. If it came damaged in a delivery or is faulty, the supervisor may return it to the supplier for a credit. If it is out of date or cannot be returned, it is disposed of as the maker's instructions and local rules say. Chemicals are never poured on the ground. Finally the stock records are corrected.
markingPoints: Removes the item from sale or use at once
Deals with any spill safely with gloves and a wet floor sign
Records the item, number, date and reason
Reports it so it can be returned to the supplier if possible
Disposes of it safely as the maker and local rules say, and corrects the records

essays.stem: What is shrinkage? Explain the causes of shrinkage in a salon and how staff can reduce it.
essays.modelAnswer: Shrinkage is stock that the salon has paid for but loses, so it is never sold or used properly. The causes include theft by clients or staff, damage when stock is dropped or stored badly, products going out of date, waste such as using too much product on a client, and mistakes in counting or in the records. Staff can reduce shrinkage in several ways. Retail stock can be kept mostly in a locked cabinet or stock room, with testers on display. Staff should record every item they take for salon use. Products should be stored and handled carefully, rotated so older stock is used first, and measured rather than poured freely. Deliveries should be checked carefully before signing. Regular stock takes help to find losses early. Any loss that cannot be explained must be reported to the manager.
markingPoints: Defines shrinkage as stock lost and not sold or properly used
Gives causes: theft, damage, expiry, waste and record mistakes
Security: locked storage and testers on display
Recording staff use, careful handling, rotation and measuring product
Checking deliveries, regular stock takes and reporting losses

essays.stem: Compare keeping stock records on paper stock cards with keeping them on a computer system. What information should each record show, and why must it be accurate?
essays.modelAnswer: On a paper stock card, staff write each movement by hand: the date, items received, items used or sold, and the balance left. It is cheap and simple, but it takes time and mistakes in adding are easy. A computer system takes items off the count when they are sold at the till and can print reports and warn when an item reaches its reorder level. It is faster, but it costs money, needs power and staff training, and still needs regular counts because it cannot see theft or damage. Both should show the product name and code, the supplier, the date, the quantity in and out, the balance, the reorder level and the cost price. The records must be accurate so the salon knows what it has, orders at the right time, finds losses quickly and has correct figures for its accounts.
markingPoints: Paper cards: simple and cheap, but slow and easy to make mistakes
Computer: updates from the till, reports and reorder warnings, but costs and still needs counts
Shows product, code, supplier, date, quantity in and out and balance
Also shows the reorder level and cost price
Accuracy is needed to order on time, find losses and keep the accounts right

essays.stem: A large bottle of peroxide falls and breaks on the stock room floor. Explain what you should do.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would warn others and keep them away from the spill, and open a window or door, or switch on the fan, to ventilate the room. I would read the safety data sheet for the product to check how to clean it up. Before touching it, I would put on chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection, and an apron if needed. I would pick up the broken glass carefully with a dustpan, not my hands, and put it in a strong, marked container. I would soak up the liquid with the material the safety data sheet says, wipe the area with plenty of water, and put out a wet floor sign. The waste is disposed of as the safety data sheet and local rules say. If any peroxide touches the skin or eyes, I would rinse with lots of clean running water and get medical help. Finally I would record and report it.
markingPoints: Keeps others away and ventilates the area
Checks the safety data sheet and puts on gloves and eye protection
Picks up glass safely with a dustpan and puts it in a marked container
Cleans up the liquid as the SDS says and puts out a wet floor sign
Gives correct first aid for skin or eye contact, and records and reports it

essays.stem: Explain how salon and spa staff can control the use of professional products, such as shampoo, hair colour and massage oil, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Professional products are used on clients during services and are not sold, so they can easily be wasted. Staff can control their use in several ways. They should follow the maker's instructions for the amount to use, and measure products with pumps, measuring cups or scales instead of pouring freely. For hair colour, they should mix only what is needed for that client. They should take only one bottle out of the stock room at a time and finish it before opening another. Each item taken from stock should be recorded on the stock card or system, and colour use can be noted on the client's record. Lids should be closed after use so products do not spill or dry out. This matters because waste raises the cost of every service, makes the salon reorder sooner, and makes it hard to see if stock is going missing.
markingPoints: Follows the maker's instructions for the amount to use
Measures products and mixes only what is needed
Opens one container at a time and closes lids after use
Records stock taken and colour used for each client
Explains that waste raises costs and hides losses

practical1.title: Receive, check, record and put away a delivery of salon and spa stock
practical1.brief: As a group, receive a delivery of stock for the Centre's salon and spa. The assessor gives you a purchase order, a delivery note and boxes of stock that include some problems, for example an item short, a damaged or leaking item, a wrong product and an item close to its expiry date. Share the work so that every member does each kind of job at least once on part of the delivery: check the boxes for damage; check each item against the delivery note and the purchase order; check the expiry dates and seals; record the goods received on the stock cards; put the stock away safely using first in, first out, with chemicals and flammable items in their proper store. Together, write the problems on the delivery note and fill in a short delivery problem report for the supervisor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Boxes of salon and spa stock from the Centre (hair, skin and nail products, consumables)
A purchase order and a delivery note from the assessor
Stock cards or a stock sheet, and a delivery problem report form
Gloves, eye protection, paper towels and a wet floor sign
A box marked for damaged stock
photos: The boxes as delivered, before opening
Items laid out and checked against the delivery note
An expiry date and a broken seal or damaged item, close up
The problems written on the delivery note
The stock cards filled in for the goods received
The shelves after putting away, new stock behind old
Chemicals and flammable products in their proper store
checklist: Checked the boxes for damage before signing
Checked items and quantities correctly against the delivery note and the purchase order
Found and recorded the short, wrong, damaged or near-expiry items
Wore gloves and handled the damaged or leaking item safely
Recorded the goods received correctly on the stock cards
Put stock away using first in, first out, with heavy items low
Stored chemicals and flammable items correctly
Helped complete a clear delivery problem report
safety: Lift boxes with a straight back and bent knees; share heavy loads
Open boxes with a safety cutter, cutting away from your body
Wear gloves and eye protection for any leaking or broken item; read its safety data sheet
Wipe up spills at once and put out a wet floor sign
Keep flammable products away from heaters and dryers

practical2.title: Carry out a stock take and prepare a purchase order
practical2.brief: As a group, carry out a stock take of the Centre's salon and spa retail shelf and dispensary. The assessor gives you a stock sheet listing each item, its cost price in J$, its stock card balance and its reorder level. Share the shelves between members so that each counts one area and then checks another member's count. Record each count at once on the stock sheet. Count damaged and out-of-date items separately. Together, compare the counts with the stock card balances, mark each variance (short or over), and work out the value of each line and the total stock value in J$. Then list every item at or below its reorder level and fill in a purchase order to bring each one up to its maximum level, for the supervisor to approve. Each member writes up and presents one part of the results to the assessor: the counts, the variances, the stock value, the items to reorder, and the damaged or expired stock. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The Centre's retail shelf and dispensary stock
Stock sheet from the assessor, with cost prices, balances, reorder and maximum levels
Stock cards for the items counted
photos: The shelves before the count, with each member's area marked
A member counting a shelf and recording on the stock sheet
The completed stock sheet with counts and variances
The stock value worked out in J$
Damaged and out-of-date items set aside and listed
The shelves left tidy, labels facing out, after the count
checklist: Counted their area accurately, shelf by shelf, and recorded each count at once
Checked another member's count and agreed any changes
Compared the counts with the stock cards and marked the variances correctly
Worked out the line values and the total stock value correctly
Listed the items at or below the reorder level
Filled in the purchase order with correct items, codes and quantities
Recorded damaged and expired items separately
Explained their part of the results clearly
safety: Use a proper step stool, not a chair or a box, to reach high shelves
Do not open chemical containers during the count
Put back each item where it came from, with heavy items low
Keep walkways clear of boxes and stock while you work
